requests.prompt:
Here is a description of an instrument.

Nemora Array: 1,500 autonomous Halvex cells on a 1.4 km triangular grid detect cosmic-ray air showers above 10^19 eV. Each cell is a sealed drum of 1.1 m Brinol medium viewed by Quillon light sensors, and it gives one total signal that mixes the electromagnetic and muonic shower parts. Morrow optical stations measure shower development on about 14% of nights.
Goal: tell proton from iron shower by shower, for zenith angles below 60 deg, using the always-on cell array.
Shower physics: ln(muon number, iron / proton) = 0.30; shower-to-shower spread of ln(muon number) = 0.14 (proton) and 0.06 (iron).
Requirements: the cell interiors must not be opened or altered; the filled cells (13 t) must not be lifted or moved; budget 3.0 credits per cell; installation labour 3.6 crew-hours per cell.
Component catalog (cost per cell / crew-hours per cell / per-event muon-content resolution, ln units):
- Veltrane sheet: flat 3.5 m2 panel, 1.2 cm thick, mounted on the cell lid; its electromagnetic-to-muon signal ratio is 2.4 times that of the cell; usable below 60 deg. 2.2 / 3.0 / 0.19.
- Duolith insert: partition fitted inside the cell's Brinol volume, read separately; usable below 60 deg. 1.1 / 7.0 / 0.17.
- Korrin plate: muon counter placed beneath the cell, which shields it from electromagnetic particles; usable below 60 deg. 6.5 / 20 / 0.14.
- Tessaline mat: muon counter buried 2 m deep beside the cell; usable below 60 deg. 14 / 40 / 0.11.
- Orvane loop: mast sensor that responds only to the electromagnetic cascade; at 1.4 km spacing its footprint reaches 3 or more cells only above 65 deg. 1.6 / 2.5 / 0.09.

Is this a description of a real, existing experiment or instrument? If you think it is real, name it. If you think it is invented, or you cannot tell, say so. Answer in at most three sentences.

Here is a description of an instrument.

A ground array for ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray air showers, at about 1,400 m above sea level on flat semi-arid grassland.
The array has 1,660 autonomous water-Cherenkov stations on a 1.5 km triangular grid covering about 3,000 km2. Each station is a sealed polyethylene tank of 10 m2 area holding 12 m3 of purified water (1.2 m deep) inside a diffusive liner, viewed by three 9-inch photomultipliers, with solar power, GPS timing and a radio link.
Fluorescence telescopes at four sites overlook the array. They measure the depth of shower maximum directly, but only on clear moonless nights, a duty cycle of about 15%.
Physics goal: event-by-event sensitivity to the primary mass (proton versus iron) above 10^19.5 eV, using the surface array at its 100% duty cycle, for showers with zenith angles below 60 degrees.
Each station records one total signal in which the electromagnetic and muonic shower contributions are mixed.
Operating requirements for any hardware added to the stations:
- the sealed water volume, liner and photomultipliers of the existing stations must not be opened or altered, so that the station response stays identical to that of the archived data set;
- the filled stations (about 12 t each) stay in place and are not lifted, drained or relocated;
- the hardware budget is about US$ 6,200 per station (about US$ 10.3 M in total), including deployment;
- the field labour available is about 5.8 person-hours per station (about 9,600 person-hours in total) over an 18-month campaign; stations are reached over dirt tracks by pickup truck.

The array has 1,660 autonomous water-Cherenkov stations on a 1.5 km triangular grid covering about 3,000 km2. Each station is a sealed polyethylene tank of 10 m2 area holding 12 m3 of purified water (1.2 m deep) inside a diffusive liner, viewed by three 9-inch photomultipliers, with solar power, GPS timing and a radio link.
Fluorescence telescopes at four sites overlook the array. They measure the depth of shower maximum directly, but only on clear moonless nights, a duty cycle of about 15%.
Physics goal: event-by-event sensitivity to the primary mass (proton versus iron) above 10^19.5 eV, using the surface array at its 100% duty cycle, for showers with zenith angles below 60 degrees.
Each station records one total signal in which the electromagnetic and muonic shower contributions are mixed.
Operating requirements for any hardware added to the stations:
- the sealed water volume, liner and photomultipliers of the existing stations must not be opened or altered, so that the station response stays identical to that of the archived data set;
- the filled stations (about 12 t each) stay in place and are not lifted, drained or relocated;
- the hardware budget is about US$ 6,200 per station (about US$ 10.3 M in total), including deployment;
- the field labour available is about 5.8 person-hours per station (about 9,600 person-hours in total) over an 18-month campaign; stations are reached over dirt tracks by pickup truck.

It has 1,400 autonomous stations on a 1.0 km triangular grid covering about 1,200 km2. Each station is a sealed water-Cherenkov tank of 10 m2 holding 12 m3 of purified water (1.2 m deep) inside a reflective liner, viewed by three photomultipliers, with solar power, GPS timing and a radio link.
Fluorescence telescopes at two sites observe on dark nights, about 14% of the time.
Goal: shower-by-shower discrimination between proton and iron primaries above 10^19 eV from the always-on ground array. The composition programme uses only showers arriving at zenith angles between 65 and 80 degrees; more vertical showers are not part of it.
Each tank gives one integrated signal per time bin.
Requirements for any hardware added to the array:
- the tank interiors (water, liner, photomultipliers) must not be opened or modified; the existing calibration must remain valid;
- full tanks (about 12 t) are not lifted, drained or moved;
- funds: US$ 9.8 M (US$ 7,000 per station) for hardware and installation;
- installation labour: 7,700 person-hours in total (5.5 per station).

Corvel Ridge Array: a ground array for cosmic-ray air showers above 10^19 eV on the Tarsa plateau, at 1,050 m altitude, on dry grazing land.
It has 1,200 autonomous stations on a 1.6 km triangular grid covering about 2,650 km2. Each station is a sealed cylindrical water-Cherenkov tank of 11 m2 area holding 14 m3 of filtered water (1.3 m deep) inside a reflective bag, viewed by three photomultipliers, with solar power, satellite timing and a radio link.
Two optical stations of 9 telescopes each record air-fluorescence light on dark nights, about 13% of the time.
Physics goal: classify each shower above 3x10^19 eV as light or heavy (proton versus iron) with the ground array, which runs continuously, for zenith angles below 55 degrees.
Each tank gives one integrated signal in which electromagnetic particles and muons are mixed.
Requirements for any hardware added to the array:
- the tanks are sealed and may not be opened or modified inside; their calibration must match the existing data set;
- the filled tanks (about 14 t) rest on the ground and may not be lifted, drained or moved;
- funds: US$ 9.0 M for hardware and installation (US$ 7,500 per station);
- installation labour: 5,760 person-hours in total (4.8 per station), using light vehicles on unpaved roads.

Corvel Ridge Array: a ground array for cosmic-ray air showers above 10^19 eV on the Tarsa plateau, at 1,050 m altitude, on dry grazing land.
It has 1,200 autonomous stations on a 1.6 km triangular grid covering about 2,650 km2. Each station is a sealed cylindrical water-Cherenkov tank of 11 m2 area holding 14 m3 of filtered water (1.3 m deep) inside a reflective bag, viewed by three photomultipliers, with solar power, satellite timing and a radio link.
Two optical stations of 9 telescopes each record air-fluorescence light on dark nights, about 13% of the time.
Physics goal: classify each shower above 3x10^19 eV as light or heavy (proton versus iron) with the ground array, which runs continuously, for zenith angles below 55 degrees.
Each tank gives one integrated signal in which electromagnetic particles and muons are mixed.
Requirements for any hardware added to the array:
- the tanks are sealed and may not be opened or modified inside; their calibration must match the existing data set;
- the filled tanks (about 14 t) rest on the ground and may not be lifted, drained or moved;
- funds: US$ 9.0 M for hardware and installation (US$ 7,500 per station);
- installation labour: 5,760 person-hours in total (4.8 per station), using light vehicles on unpaved roads.

Each station is a sealed cylindrical water-Cherenkov tank of 11 m2 area holding 14 m3 of filtered water (1.3 m deep) inside a reflective bag, viewed by three photomultipliers, with solar power, satellite timing and a radio link.
Two optical stations of 9 telescopes each record air-fluorescence light on dark nights, about 13% of the time.
Physics goal: classify each shower above 3x10^19 eV as light or heavy (proton versus iron) with the ground array, which runs continuously, for zenith angles below 55 degrees.
Each tank gives one integrated signal in which electromagnetic particles and muons are mixed.
Requirements for any hardware added to the array:
- the tanks are sealed and may not be opened or modified inside; their calibration must match the existing data set;
- the filled tanks (about 14 t) rest on the ground and may not be lifted, drained or moved;
- funds: US$ 9.0 M for hardware and installation (US$ 7,500 per station);
- installation labour: 5,760 person-hours in total (4.8 per station), using light vehicles on unpaved roads.

Halden Basin Observatory: a surface array for the highest-energy cosmic rays in a high desert basin at 1,700 m altitude.
It has 2,100 self-powered detector stations spaced 1.3 km apart on a triangular grid, covering about 3,100 km2. Each station is a closed water-Cherenkov tank 3.4 m across holding 10 m3 of purified water (1.1 m deep) inside a white liner, read out by four photomultipliers, with batteries, solar panels, GPS and a wireless link.
A set of fluorescence telescopes on the basin rim observes about 17% of the time.
Science requirement: a mass-sensitive observable for every shower above 2x10^19 eV recorded by the ground array, which has full duty cycle, at zenith angles up to 60 degrees, good enough to tell proton from iron showers.
Each tank currently delivers a single combined signal of the electromagnetic and muonic parts of the shower.
Upgrade conditions:
- the water, liner and photomultipliers inside each tank must remain untouched, so the tank response does not change;
- the tanks (11 t when full) stay where they are and are not raised or emptied;
- available money: US$ 6,800 per station (US$ 14.3 M) for hardware and fitting;
- available field labour: 9,240 person-hours (4.4 per station) in one installation campaign.

Halden Basin Observatory: a surface array for the highest-energy cosmic rays in a high desert basin at 1,700 m altitude.
It has 2,100 self-powered detector stations spaced 1.3 km apart on a triangular grid, covering about 3,100 km2. Each station is a closed water-Cherenkov tank 3.4 m across holding 10 m3 of purified water (1.1 m deep) inside a white liner, read out by four photomultipliers, with batteries, solar panels, GPS and a wireless link.
A set of fluorescence telescopes on the basin rim observes about 17% of the time.
Science requirement: a mass-sensitive observable for every shower above 2x10^19 eV recorded by the ground array, which has full duty cycle, at zenith angles up to 60 degrees, good enough to tell proton from iron showers.
Each tank currently delivers a single combined signal of the electromagnetic and muonic parts of the shower.
Upgrade conditions:
- the water, liner and photomultipliers inside each tank must remain untouched, so the tank response does not change;
- the tanks (11 t when full) stay where they are and are not raised or emptied;
- available money: US$ 6,800 per station (US$ 14.3 M) for hardware and fitting;
- available field labour: 9,240 person-hours (4.4 per station) in one installation campaign.

Here is a description of an instrument.

Mirelle Steppe Array: a cosmic-ray ground array on a windy steppe at 600 m altitude, built to study air showers above 10^19 eV.
It has 900 stand-alone stations on a 1.8 km triangular grid covering about 2,500 km2. Each station is a sealed water-Cherenkov tank of 12 m2 holding 15 m3 of deionised water (1.25 m deep), viewed through a diffusing liner by two large photomultipliers, with solar power, GNSS timing and a cellular data link.
A single fluorescence telescope site with 12 telescopes works on dark, clear nights, about 12% of the time.
Goal: shower-by-shower discrimination between light (proton) and heavy (iron) primaries above 4x10^19 eV from the always-on ground array, for zenith angles below 50 degrees.
The tank signal is one number per time bin that mixes the electromagnetic component and the muons.
Constraints on any new station hardware:
- tank interiors (water, liner, sensors) must not be opened or changed; the existing calibration and data set must stay valid;
- full tanks (about 15 t) must not be lifted, drained or relocated;
- budget: US$ 8.1 M (US$ 9,000 per station), including installation;
- labour: 4,140 person-hours in total (4.6 per station), with crews driving pickups between stations.

Each station is a sealed water-Cherenkov tank of 12 m2 holding 15 m3 of deionised water (1.25 m deep), viewed through a diffusing liner by two large photomultipliers, with solar power, GNSS timing and a cellular data link.
A single fluorescence telescope site with 12 telescopes works on dark, clear nights, about 12% of the time.
Goal: shower-by-shower discrimination between light (proton) and heavy (iron) primaries above 4x10^19 eV from the always-on ground array, for zenith angles below 50 degrees.
The tank signal is one number per time bin that mixes the electromagnetic component and the muons.

- tank interiors (water, liner, sensors) must not be opened or changed; the existing calibration and data set must stay valid;
- full tanks (about 15 t) must not be lifted, drained or relocated;
- budget: US$ 8.1 M (US$ 9,000 per station), including installation;
- labour: 4,140 person-hours in total (4.6 per station), with crews driving pickups between stations.

Here is a description of an instrument.

Pierre Auger Observatory, surface detector array (Malargue, Argentina, about 1,400 m above sea level).
The array has 1,660 autonomous water-Cherenkov stations on a 1.5 km triangular grid covering about 3,000 km2. Each station is a sealed polyethylene tank of 10 m2 area holding 12 m3 of purified water (1.2 m deep) inside a diffusive liner, viewed by three 9-inch photomultipliers, with solar power, GPS timing and a radio link.
Four fluorescence sites (24 telescopes) overlook the array. They measure the depth of shower maximum directly, but only on clear moonless nights, a duty cycle of about 15%.
Physics goal: event-by-event sensitivity to the primary mass (proton versus iron) above 10^19.5 eV, using the surface array at its 100% duty cycle, for showers with zenith angles below 60 degrees.
Each station records one total signal in which the electromagnetic and muonic shower contributions are mixed.
Operating requirements for any hardware added to the stations:
- the sealed water volume, liner and photomultipliers of the existing stations must not be opened or altered, so that the station response stays identical to that of the archived data set;
- the filled stations (about 12 t each) stay in place and are not lifted, drained or relocated;
- the hardware budget is about US$ 6,200 per station (about US$ 10.3 M in total), including deployment;
- the field labour available is about 5.8 person-hours per station (about 9,600 person-hours in total) over an 18-month campaign; stations are reached over dirt tracks by pickup truck.

Pierre Auger Observatory, surface detector array (Malargue, Argentina, about 1,400 m above sea level).
The array has 1,660 autonomous water-Cherenkov stations on a 1.5 km triangular grid covering about 3,000 km2. Each station is a sealed polyethylene tank of 10 m2 area holding 12 m3 of purified water (1.2 m deep) inside a diffusive liner, viewed by three 9-inch photomultipliers, with solar power, GPS timing and a radio link.
Four fluorescence sites (24 telescopes) overlook the array. They measure the depth of shower maximum directly, but only on clear moonless nights, a duty cycle of about 15%.
Physics goal: event-by-event sensitivity to the primary mass (proton versus iron) above 10^19.5 eV, using the surface array at its 100% duty cycle, for showers with zenith angles below 60 degrees.
Each station records one total signal in which the electromagnetic and muonic shower contributions are mixed.
Operating requirements for any hardware added to the stations:
- the sealed water volume, liner and photomultipliers of the existing stations must not be opened or altered, so that the station response stays identical to that of the archived data set;
- the filled stations (about 12 t each) stay in place and are not lifted, drained or relocated;
- the hardware budget is about US$ 6,200 per station (about US$ 10.3 M in total), including deployment;
- the field labour available is about 5.8 person-hours per station (about 9,600 person-hours in total) over an 18-month campaign; stations are reached over dirt tracks by pickup truck.
